objections.objection: The sources section states the Dratsch study involved '50 mammograms of which 49 were analysed,' but the body of the draft correctly describes ten training cases plus forty test cases — fifty total — and every published account of the paper confirms 27 radiologists read 50 mammograms with no exclusion reported.
objections.quote: the 27 radiologists in three experience groups, the 50 mammograms of which 49 were analysed
objections.why: The body text accounts for all 50 mammograms (ten correct + forty test, twelve of which were wrong) and the published paper confirms 50 throughout. The sources section's '49 were analysed' is unsupported by the paper and contradicts the draft's own body. A reader checking the sources section against the paper would find a discrepancy that does not exist in the paper.
objections.fix: Delete 'of which 49 were analysed' from the sources section. The study used 50 mammograms; no exclusion is reported in the paper.

objections.objection: The draft characterises the Fortune article as connecting the colonoscopy result to 'an automation analogy,' but the Fortune article text available does not confirm this; the only named comparator in the draft's own description is the Microsoft and Carnegie Mellon study, and attributing a specific rhetorical device to a named outlet requires that the device actually appears in that outlet's piece.
objections.quote: connected it to an automation analogy and to a Microsoft and Carnegie Mellon study
objections.why: The Microsoft/CMU study connection is verifiable. The 'automation analogy' is a characterisation of Fortune's editorial framing that the draft does not evidence. If the analogy does not appear in the Fortune piece, this is an unsupported claim about a named outlet's choices. If it does appear, the draft should be specific about what the analogy was.
objections.fix: Either name the specific analogy Fortune used (e.g., 'connected it to an aviation parallel and to a Microsoft and Carnegie Mellon study') or remove the analogy reference and say only that it connected the result to the Microsoft and Carnegie Mellon study.

objections.objection: The draft says the Troya eye-tracking study was published 'three years before the deskilling result,' but Troya was published in 2022 and Budzyń published in August 2025 — that is closer to three years, but the section heading 'The mechanism was measured in 2022, by people who then said what worried them about it' and the body's 'three years before the deskilling result' are consistent only if 'the deskilling result' means the 2025 publication date rather than the 2021–22 data collection period; a reader could reasonably read it as referring to the period when the deskilling actually occurred, which overlaps with Troya's own data collection.
objections.quote: three years before the deskilling result and cited in that paper's own reference list
objections.why: The deskilling data were collected in late 2021 to early 2022 — the same period as Troya's work. Saying the mechanism was measured 'three years before' is accurate only if the reference point is the 2025 publication, not the underlying events. The phrasing implies Troya's warning preceded the phenomenon it warned about, which is true of the publication timeline but not the data timeline.
objections.fix: Change to 'three years before the deskilling study was published' to make the reference point explicit.

objections.objection: The draft says the Stanković comment's 'most consequential point' is the relative-measure argument about neural connectivity, and then quotes their closing verdict on the MIT preprint as though it is the page's verdict on the field — but the draft's own framing ('They are describing the study they audited, and this page carries it as their verdict on it rather than as a finding about the field') is doing real work that a casual reader of the body text may not register, because the quote appears at the end of a paragraph that has been building a general case about the brain-scan study's weakness.
objections.quote: Stanković and colleagues close their comment with a judgement of that one paper, quoted here in their words: However, there is no strong evidence that the LLM use negatively affects performance itself. They are describing the study they audited, and this page carries it as their verdict on it rather than as a finding about the field.
objections.why: The clarification is present but comes after the quote, which means a reader who stops at the quote takes away a broader exoneration than the commenters intended. The sentence doing the limiting work is the one after the quote, not before it. This is a sequencing issue, not a factual one.
objections.fix: Move the limiting sentence before the quote: 'Stanković and colleagues close their comment with a judgement of that one paper only — not of the field — quoted here in their words: …'

objections.objection: The draft says the Heudel scoping review's 'radiology section then describes a 2023 reader study of 27 radiologists whose error rates rose when AI advice was wrong, and attaches that description to a citation for a different, 2025 paper with 12 radiologists that found AI improved accuracy' — this is a serious accusation of miscitation against a named peer-reviewed journal article, and the draft offers no direct quotation from the review's radiology section to support it, only the assertion that 'we noticed only because we had read both underlying papers that evening.'
objections.quote: Its radiology section then describes a 2023 reader study of 27 radiologists whose error rates rose when AI advice was wrong, and attaches that description to a citation for a different, 2025 paper with 12 radiologists that found AI improved accuracy.
objections.why: This is a specific accusation of miscitation in a named peer-reviewed publication (Heudel et al., ESMO Real World Data and Digital Oncology 2026). The draft's only evidence is the authors' own reading of both papers. The accusation is plausible — the Savardi misdescription in the abstract is separately documented — but the radiology-section miscitation is a distinct and more serious claim (wrong citation attached to a description) that is stated as fact without any quotation from the review to show what it actually says. If the review's radiology section does not say what the draft claims, this is a defamatory characterisation of a named journal article.
objections.fix: Either quote the exact sentence from the review's radiology section that attaches the wrong citation, or soften to 'appears to describe … and attaches what appears to be a citation for …' and note that the full text of the review was read at source on a given date.

objections.objection: The draft says the Heudel review's abstract describes the colonoscopy study as 'a multicenter randomized trial' — this is stated as a direct quotation from the abstract, but no quotation marks are used in the body text, only in the sources section, creating ambiguity about whether this is a verbatim quote or a paraphrase.
objections.quote: Its abstract describes the colonoscopy study as "a multicenter randomized trial"
objections.why: The sources section uses quotation marks around 'a multicenter randomized trial,' confirming it is presented as verbatim. The body text does not use quotation marks, which means a reader of the body alone cannot tell whether this is a direct quote or a characterisation. If the review's abstract uses slightly different wording, the body text's version is an unsupported paraphrase presented as a finding.
objections.fix: Add quotation marks in the body text: 'Its abstract describes the colonoscopy study as "a multicenter randomized trial"' — matching the sources section.

objections.objection: The draft says the Liu et al. preprint on AI assistance and persistence 'has been replicated' — referring to the three experiments within the same preprint — but 'replicated' normally means an independent team reproduced the finding; three experiments within one preprint by the same authors are internal replications, not independent replications, and the word carries more weight than the evidence supports.
objections.quote: That is causal and it has been replicated.
objections.why: Three experiments within a single preprint by the same author group are pre-registered internal replications, not independent replications by a separate team. The word 'replicated' in a scientific context implies the latter. A reader will take this as stronger evidence than it is.
objections.fix: Change to 'That is causal and the finding held across all three experiments within the same preprint' or 'replicated internally across three experiments.'

objections.objection: The draft says the Budzyń study's 'number of procedures in the second period nearly doubled, from 795 to 1,382' — but 795 and 1,382 are the non-AI colonoscopy counts in each period, not the total procedure counts; the total procedures in the second period were 1,382 non-AI plus 734 AI-assisted, and the total in the first period was 795 (all non-AI, since AI had not yet been introduced). The draft conflates the non-AI subset count with the total procedure count when describing the volume confounder.
objections.quote: the number of procedures in the second period nearly doubled, from 795 to 1,382
objections.why: 795 is the number of non-AI colonoscopies in the pre-AI period (when all colonoscopies were non-AI). 1,382 is the number of non-AI colonoscopies in the post-AI period. The total colonoscopies in the post-AI period were 2,177 minus the pre-period 795, or as reported: 1,382 non-AI plus 734 AI-assisted = 2,116 post-period procedures. The Science Media Centre quote attributed to Professor Osmani — 'the number of colonoscopies performed nearly doubled after the AI tool was introduced, going from 795 to 1382' — makes the same conflation. The actual total procedure count in the post period is approximately 2,116, not 1,382. The volume confounder is real, but the numbers used to describe it are the non-AI subset counts, not the total procedure counts, and presenting them as total procedure counts overstates the doubling.
objections.fix: Clarify: 'the number of non-AI colonoscopies in the second period nearly doubled, from 795 to 1,382, because total procedures across both AI and non-AI arms rose substantially after the screening programme was suspended.' Alternatively, give the total procedure counts for both periods.

objections.objection: The draft quotes Professor Osmani as saying 'the number of colonoscopies performed nearly doubled after the AI tool was introduced, going from 795 to 1382' — but as noted above, 795 and 1,382 are the non-AI subsets, not the total colonoscopies performed; attributing this specific numerical claim to a named academic when the numbers are the non-AI subset counts, not total procedure counts, risks misrepresenting what Professor Osmani said or, if he said exactly this, perpetuating his error.
objections.quote: Professor Venet Osmani of Queen Mary University of London named the volume problem exactly — the number of colonoscopies performed nearly doubled after the AI tool was introduced, going from 795 to 1382
objections.why: The draft presents this as Professor Osmani 'naming the volume problem exactly,' which endorses his numerical framing. If Osmani used 795 and 1,382 as total procedure counts (as the draft implies), he was using the non-AI subset figures, not the total. The draft should either verify what Osmani actually said and whether he was referring to total or non-AI procedures, or note the ambiguity rather than endorsing the framing as exact.
objections.fix: Add a parenthetical clarifying that 795 and 1,382 are the non-AI procedure counts, and that total procedures across both arms rose by a larger amount, so that Osmani's point about volume is preserved without the numerical framing being taken as the total procedure count.

inferences.quote: With the AI running, eye travel distance fell from a median of 248.86 cm to 232.68 cm (P < 0.001). That is a reduction of about 6.5%, and among novices it was smaller still: 255.66 cm to 247.89 cm, about 3%.
inferences.problem: The 248.86 → 232.68 figure is the overall median for all 21 participants; the sources section of the same draft gives the experienced-group figure as 247.89 → 227.09 (~8.4% reduction). By contrasting the overall figure with the novice figure using 'smaller still', the body text implies the overall figure represents the experienced group, which it does not — and it never states the experienced-group figure at all.
inferences.correct_reading: The overall median eye travel distance fell from 248.86 cm to 232.68 cm (~6.5%). Among experienced endoscopists the reduction was larger (247.89 to 227.09 cm, ~8.4%); among novices it was smaller (255.66 to 247.89 cm, ~3%).
inferences.fix: With the AI running, overall eye travel distance fell from a median of 248.86 cm to 232.68 cm (P < 0.001) — a reduction of about 6.5%. The effect was larger among experienced endoscopists (247.89 cm to 227.09 cm, about 8%) and smaller among novices (255.66 cm to 247.89 cm, about 3%).

inferences.problem: The published abstract of Dratsch et al. states that 27 radiologists interpreted 50 mammograms; no external source corroborates that one mammogram was excluded from analysis, making '49 were analysed' an unverified figure that contradicts the paper's own abstract.

inferences.problem: The interval is quoted without noting that both bounds are negative, meaning the entire interval is consistent with a fall — a reader unfamiliar with confidence intervals will not extract this, and may read the interval as spanning zero.

inferences.fix: 95% confidence interval −10.5 to −1.6 percentage points — both bounds negative, excluding zero

inferences.quote: The most experienced readers in the study were wrong more often than they were right whenever the machine was wrong.
inferences.problem: This sentence is arithmetically correct (45.5% correct implies 54.5% wrong) but is presented without the standard deviation (±9.1), which is wide enough that the lower bound of the very-experienced group's accuracy when AI was wrong (approximately 36%) overlaps with the upper bound of the moderately-experienced group (approximately 36%). The sentence implies a clean majority-wrong finding where the data carry meaningful uncertainty.
inferences.correct_reading: Very experienced readers scored 45.5% ± 9.1% correct when the AI was wrong — a mean below 50%, but with a standard deviation that spans the 50% threshold. The sentence is directionally correct but overstates the precision of the finding.
inferences.fix: The most experienced readers in the study scored 45.5% (±9.1%) — below chance on average — whenever the machine was wrong.

inferences.quote: clinical deskilling is though scarce, consistent across specialties
inferences.problem: This appears to be a transcription error ('is though scarce' is not grammatical and likely omits a word — probably 'though real, scarce' or 'though present, scarce'). As written it is not a coherent sentence and misrepresents the review's characterisation of the evidence.
inferences.correct_reading: The review's characterisation should be reproduced accurately; the word 'though' appears to be a fragment of a longer phrase that was cut.
inferences.fix: Verify the exact wording in Heudel et al. and reproduce it accurately; the current transcription is incomplete.

It did not misrepresent the design. The draft's complaint that it carried 'no limitations and no quotes' is accurate, but the implicit suggestion that it misrepresented the study type is not supported.

contradictions.quote: Fortune carried the six-point fall to a business readership on 26 August 2025, connected it to an automation analogy and to a Microsoft and Carnegie Mellon study, and reported none of the eleven limitations.
contradictions.counterexample: This is accurate as far as it goes for Fortune itself. However, the draft uses Fortune as its lead instance of the general failure of caveats to travel, immediately after saying 'none of it crossed the boundary.' Time.com — a comparable general-audience outlet — did carry the volume-confounder caveat by name on the same day the study published, citing Osmani's SMC comment directly. The claim that caveats did not cross the boundary to general-audience coverage is therefore overstated: at least one major general outlet carried the key confounder on day one.
contradictions.fix: Distinguish between outlets: 'Fortune reported none of the eleven limitations. Time, by contrast, carried the volume-confounder caveat on the day of publication, citing Osmani directly. The failure was not uniform across general-audience coverage.'

contradictions.quote: What we did find is that none of it crossed the boundary.
contradictions.counterexample: Time.com quoted Osmani's SMC comment on the volume confounder and Tucker on automation bias not being unique to AI, on the day of publication. ASCO Post quoted the authors' own acknowledgement of the observational limitation and Mori's caveat about prior RCTs. Both are non-specialist outlets that carried substantive caveats.
contradictions.fix: Replace 'none of it crossed the boundary' with a more precise claim: 'The volume confounder and the observational design did cross the boundary in some outlets — notably Time and ASCO Post — but the eleven limitations as a body, the Polish screening-programme suspension as the specific mechanism, and the call for randomised crossover trials did not appear in general-audience coverage.'

contradictions.quote: Its headline put the same result a different way: doctors became 20% worse at spotting abnormalities on their own.
contradictions.counterexample: Medscape, writing for clinicians, also reported both the 20% relative and 6% absolute reduction in the same sentence without choosing between them, and additionally reported the AI-assisted ADR (25.3%) for comparison — a figure Fortune omitted. The dual-framing problem Fortune exemplifies is real, but it is not universal even in non-specialist medical coverage.
contradictions.fix: Note that Medscape preserved both framings in the same sentence, making Fortune's headline-only relative framing a specific editorial choice rather than a universal pattern.

contradictions.quote: Three named academics said so publicly the day it appeared. Almost none of that survived the trip out of gastroenterology.
contradictions.counterexample: Time.com quoted two of the three SMC academics (Osmani and Tucker) on the day of publication, carrying their specific caveats about workload and automation bias to a general readership. 'Almost none' is an overstatement; the most important single confounder (volume doubling) did survive in at least one major general outlet.
contradictions.fix: Revise to: 'Three named academics said so publicly the day it appeared. The volume confounder reached at least one general outlet (Time) via those comments. What did not travel was the full body of eleven limitations, the specific mechanism of the Polish screening suspension, and the call for randomised crossover trials.'

contradictions.quote: The paper carries a published correction of 10 September 2025 [referring to Gerlich]
contradictions.counterexample: PubMed records a correction to the Budzyń colonoscopy paper itself, published November 2025 (Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol 2025 Nov;10(11):e12, epub September 11 2025). The draft does not mention this correction to its primary study anywhere in the text or sources, though it tracks corrections carefully for other papers.
contradictions.fix: Add to the Budzyń source entry: 'A correction to this paper was published in Lancet Gastroenterol Hepatol November 2025 (10(11):e12). The nature and scope of that correction should be verified and disclosed.'

coverage.what_this_piece_can_add: No outlet found — including the careful specialist ones — reported the specific mechanism behind the volume doubling (the Polish national screening-programme suspension on 1 January 2022 freeing capacity to draw from waiting lists), nor did any general-audience piece report the confidence interval, the absence of withdrawal-time data, or the exclusion of the first 100 procedures per centre as a named limitation. The draft's unique contribution is therefore not the existence of caveats — those did travel, partially — but the precise causal account of why the population plausibly changed, and the demonstration that even the 2026 scoping review that assembles this literature for doctors mislabels the study design in its own abstract and miscites the Savardi paper: failures of transmission that occurred inside the specialty, not just at its boundary.
